note: Scaffolding for a client fixture that stands up more than one Nestor deployment. Extracted persona-free from the two-desks fixture on claude/nestor-intake-repo-review-icanwi; that branch keeps its own walk-through and its findings. This file will grow when the client's fixture lands on the same PR.

decisions.question: Bring the two-desks work over by copying the fixture, or by extracting the scaffolding?
decisions.commitment: Extract. demo/desks.py holds how to stand a desk up and how to say a claim failed, and knows nothing about whose desk it is.
decisions.why: The persona and the findings belong to the branch that earned them, and copying the fixture would have this branch carrying an Attercliffe walk-through nobody asked it to review. It also would have duplicated the machinery in two places before either had merged. Extracting means the client fixture starts from a module with a test rather than from a file it has to gut.

decisions.question: What is the module actually for, if the demo it came from is not here?
decisions.commitment: The three process globals: the ledger path, the store and the matcher. Desk.activate sets all three together and every accessor calls it first.
decisions.why: A fixture that stands two desks up and sets these once has not built two desks — it has built one desk that changes its mind about which store it is. The failure is quiet: both desks' decisions land in whichever chain was configured last, and any count taken afterwards is a true number about the wrong thing. That is not hypothetical; it is what the first fixture written against this arrangement did, and it reported one desk's total as the other's. Switching desks is now one call you cannot half-do rather than three you can.

decisions.question: Why install the matcher process-wide rather than only passing matcher= to each call?
decisions.why: nestor.ui has no matcher of its own and no field for one, so every write the surface makes normalizes with whatever is installed. Passing matcher= covers the library calls a fixture makes and misses every seal and rejection made at the surface — which is where the human decisions are, and therefore the only ones worth a fixture. The constraint that comes with it is stated in the module docstring rather than hidden: one process holds one matcher, so two custom-matcher desks in one interpreter are two desks taking turns, and scripts/two_instances.py is what to reach for when that is not good enough.

decisions.question: Does the module get a test when it has no fixture using it yet?
decisions.commitment: Yes — tests/test_desks.py, six tests, including one that reproduces the failure the module exists to prevent.
decisions.why: Otherwise it is scaffolding with no consumer and nothing holding it to its claims until the client fixture arrives. The last test sets the globals directly, the way a fixture that had never heard of Desk would, and asserts both desks' decisions land in one chain — so the thing being prevented is executable rather than described.

decisions.question: The client's fixture — a scripted walk-through like shoebox.py, or something else?
decisions.commitment: Something else. demo/big_jim.py is a standing desk driven a command at a time, not an argument with an ending.
decisions.why: shoebox.py and sixty_seconds.py both make a case and stop; their value is that they assert and exit non-zero. This one is for a person playing the verifier, so it needs a store that survives between runs and a surface that takes decisions when they arrive rather than in a fixed order. It is the first fixture here that is a tool rather than a demonstration, and it is the first consumer of demo/desks.py — which is how the scaffolding got exercised by something other than its own test.

decisions.question: How does the fixture avoid sealing on the operator's behalf?
decisions.commitment: seal requires --verifier on the command line: no default, no $USER fallback, and no route to sealed from draft().
decisions.why: TODO.md §5.1 — a name a script supplied is not a human checking anything. The machine-side verb (draft) cannot reach status=sealed at all, and the human-side verb refuses to run without a name someone typed. On a used-car lot the incentive to blur that is unusually strong, which is the reason the fixture is set there.

decisions.question: Why key on the last six of the VIN rather than the whole thing?
decisions.commitment: KEY_TAIL = 6, fixed before anything was measured, and the collision risk is reported by `state` rather than hidden.
decisions.why: Nobody on a forecourt reads all seventeen characters, and the last six are the sequential production number — the part that actually distinguishes two cars off the same line. It is a real trade-off, not a safe default: two vehicles can share a tail, and a disclosure served for the wrong car is the exact failure this product exists to prevent. So `state` counts keys held by more than one row and prints them in red. A number tuned until the demo looked good would be corpus-fitting wearing a method's clothes.

decisions.question: Where does the review desk's list of defects come from?
decisions.commitment: Parsed from the `### 6.N` headings of IDEAS.md in this checkout, and nowhere else.
decisions.why: Same rule scripts/dogfood_store.py states and gates: a memory whose rows came from somewhere nobody can see is not an audit trail. A desk listing defects an agent remembered would be exactly that. An entry is open because its own heading says open, not because this module has a view — which is also why it disagrees with a naive grep: `grep -cE '^### 6.[0-9]+ .*open'` counts 11 because §6.7's *title* is 'while the store is open', while the parser reads the status field and correctly counts 10.

decisions.question: Does `bearing` — plain-English risk in, relevant defect out — actually work?
decisions.commitment: No, and the command says so on screen rather than presenting the ranking as an answer.
decisions.why: Measured: 'two people in the family share the same name' returns §6.35 top at 0.062, when the entry actually about two people sharing a name is §6.37. 'an alias for somebody nobody has verified' tops out at 0.062. The one query that scored (0.583) was phrased in the finding's own words. DefectMatcher weights identifier tokens above prose by design, and a risk described in plain English shares almost no identifiers with a defect title — so this is the matcher working as specified on input it was never meant for. It is left in because the browse view is still useful for finding candidates to read, and because a retrieval that scores 0.06 while looking confident is worth having on the record. Nothing is served: every row is a draft, so tier 1 is empty by construction and the bad ranking cannot reach an answer.

decisions.question: Do those six tests hold anything?
decisions.commitment: Proven by mutation. Dropping the matcher line from activate() turns two red; dropping the ledger line turns three red.
decisions.why: A gate nobody has watched fail is a description. Also recorded: the first version of this file assumed a proposal writes a ledger line and asserted on chains after calling propose(). It does not — a draft is not a decision and appends nothing — so four tests failed for a reason that was the test's error rather than the module's, and they were rewritten to seal first. And the SerialMatcher used here keeps every digit it finds, so an early restatement of 'ward 6' keyed to 44716 and missed; that was the test's fault too, and the assertion now avoids stray digits and says why.
